title: Why Tall Buildings Use Revolving Doors
sources: ASHRAE Handbook, Fundamentals: 'stack effect' (warm indoor air rises in tall buildings in cold weather, drawing outside air in at the lower floors and creating pressure on ground-floor doors)
Cullum, Feinberg et al., MIT 'Modeling Revolving Door Usage' (2006): revolving doors exchange far less air than swinging doors because they are never open straight through

lines.text: Why do tall buildings use revolving doors?
It's not for style, it's because of the air.
In winter, the warm air inside a tall building rises, just like in a chimney,
and that pulls cold air in at the bottom, hard.
Open a normal door down there, and the wind can slam it or hold it shut.
A revolving door is never open all the way through,
so the building stays sealed, and much less heat escapes.
Engineers call it the stack effect.
So next time you push one, you're holding back a chimney.
lines.caps: NEXT TIME YOU *PUSH | HOLDING BACK A *CHIMNEY
